hints: Think about what the letters H, I and V stand for - H relates to the host species affected and V tells you the type of pathogen.
walkthrough:
Decoding The Abbreviation**
HIV is a virus that infects humans and attacks cells of the immune system. H stands for human, I for immunodeficiency meaning failure of the immune system, and V for virus.

hints: Start by scanning all eight boxes in Fig. 4.1 and sorting them into decrease versus increase - which pattern is more common?
Now look for the regions that do not follow the main pattern and note their letters and percentage values.
Compare the size of the decreases to find the largest and smallest percentage decreases - check E and G carefully.
Remember you need paired evidence for full credit, so pick specific numbers of new infections and percentages to quote alongside each trend you state.
walkthrough:
The Overall Trend**
Count the labels. Six regions A, C, E, F, G, H all show a decrease, so most of the world shows a fall in new infections. This is your first conclusion.

Spotting The Exceptions**
Two regions go the opposite way. B shows a 29% increase to 150000 new infections and D shows a 10% increase to 20000 new infections. In data questions always state exceptions separately.

Ranking The Decreases**
Among the decreases, look at the percentages. E at 28% decrease is the biggest fall, despite still having the highest absolute number at 800000. G at 7% decrease is the smallest fall. Quoting both the letter, percentage and number gives precise evidence.

Final answer: In most regions there was a decrease in new infections between 2010 and 2018; exceptions were B (Eastern Europe and Central Asia) with 29% increase and D (Middle East and North Africa) with 10% increase; largest percentage decrease was 28% in E (East and Southern Africa, 800000 new infections); smallest percentage decrease was 7% in G (Latin America, 100000 new infections).

hints: Recall what HIV destroys and what that means for the overall strength of the immune system - what word describes infections like TB that take advantage of this?
Think about the normal coordinating role of T-helper cells - what chemical signal do they release to activate other immune cells?
Follow the two main arms that fail: how does loss of that signal affect phagocytes, and how does it affect B-lymphocytes?
Link each failure to the outcome for the TB bacterium - less destruction by phagocytosis and fewer antibodies.
walkthrough:
Why TB Is Opportunistic**
HIV destroys T-helper cells, leaving the immune system weakened. TB bacteria, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, are normally controlled but can now establish infection. That is why TB is called an opportunistic disease.

Loss Of Coordination**
T-helper cells normally recognise antigen and secrete cytokines. Cytokines stimulate phagocytes to become more active and stimulate specific B-lymphocytes to divide by mitosis to form plasma cells and memory cells.

Two Failed Defences**
With fewer T-helper cells, less cytokine is released. So there is less phagocytosis of TB bacteria and fewer B-lymphocytes activated, meaning fewer plasma cells and fewer antibodies secreted. With fewer pathogens destroyed, latent TB can also become reactivated and active TB is more likely.

Final answer: TB is an opportunistic infection of a weakened immune system; fewer T-helper cells give a less effective primary immune response; less cytokine secreted so less stimulation of phagocytosis and fewer B-lymphocytes stimulated to divide by mitosis into plasma cells; fewer antibodies secreted so fewer TB pathogens destroyed.

hints: Look at Fig. 4.2 and the white arrows - what physical effect does blood in the pericardium sac have on the ventricle walls?
If the ventricles are squeezed from outside, how does that change how much they can fill during diastole and how forcefully they can contract in systole?
Link a smaller volume ejected per beat to blood pressure and to blood flow to the lungs and body - what happens to oxygen delivery?
Think why breathing faster would help if less oxygen is reaching the blood and tissues.
walkthrough:
Compression Prevents Filling**
The pericardium sac filled with blood presses inward on the ventricles. The ventricles cannot expand fully in diastole, so their volume is reduced and less blood fills them.

Less Blood Pumped Lowers Pressure**
With less blood inside, ventricular contraction is less powerful and less blood is ejected per beat. That means reduced stroke volume and cardiac output to the pulmonary circulation and systemic circulation, which is measured as low blood pressure.

Less Gas Exchange Triggers Faster Breathing**
Less blood flow through the lungs means less oxygen diffuses into the blood and less carbon dioxide diffuses out, so less oxygen is delivered to tissues including cardiac muscle. The body compensates by increasing breathing rate to try to increase oxygen absorption in the lungs.

Final answer: Blood in pericardium compresses ventricles so ventricular volume is reduced and ventricles cannot fill fully; less blood leaves ventricles per cardiac cycle so ventricular systole is weaker; less blood pumped to pulmonary and systemic circulation, lowering blood pressure; less oxygen diffuses into blood and less oxygen delivered to tissues, so breathing rate increases to increase oxygen uptake.
